lecture.title: Semantics: The Study of Meaning
lecture.scope: Lecture 7. Original examples apply the supplied concepts. Reversed definitions and misleading illustrations are corrected; contextual assumptions are stated where they affect classification.
lecture.exam_alignment: Concept-based practice. No past paper or official examination blueprint was supplied.
lecture.answer_model: Single best answer. answer_id refers to an option id, not its displayed position. Preserve option ids when shuffling.
lecture.display_guidance: In learning mode, display explanation followed by example after the learner answers. Source slides and clarification notes can appear in a reference panel.
lecture.terminology: Extension/intension use an introductory category-based account. Opposition types are tested in specified uses; semantic-role labels are an introductory inventory rather than a claim that all theories use identical divisions.

references.title: Intension
references.supports: Intension concerns descriptive content determining applicability; extension concerns the class of applicable objects rather than a personal image.

references.title: The Lexical Perspective
references.publication: The Discipline of Organizing: 4th Professional Edition
references.supports: The more specific class is named by a hyponym, and the more general class by a hypernym; the slide’s reversed wording is corrected.

references.title: Metonymy
references.supports: Metonymy refers through an associated expression, such as an institution for its officials.

references.title: Metonymy
references.supports: The introductory contrast foregrounds association within a frame for metonymy and mapping across frames for metaphor.

references.title: Cop
references.supports: Cop is an informal term for a police officer; that lexical equivalence is not by itself an example of metonymy.

references.title: 7.6 Events and thematic roles
references.supports: Role inventories can distinguish agents, themes, experiencers, and non-intentional causers; grammatical subject does not mean agent in every sentence.

clarifications.note: Lexical semantics concerns word and morpheme meanings. The slide’s larger-than-word definition is corrected rather than used as an answer key.

Intension is not merely personal imagery or association. Extension is the applicable set in a domain. Fictional reference challenges a simple account, not every semantic theory. Deserts need not be hot or sandy, and material steel is not imposed as a necessary feature of all needle senses.

Shared properties do not establish synonymy. Occupational words are not assigned gender restrictions from stereotypes. Associations and feature analysis remain valid research interests with appropriate limits.
A synonym-like gloss list does not itself enumerate distinct senses. Selectional oddness is assessed under an ordinary literal reading and can change with fiction or personification.

Near-synonyms are not assumed substitutable in all contexts. Complementarity is illustrated in a stipulated binary domain. Buy/sell and teacher/pupil are relational rather than gradable temperature-style opposites.

Homonymy/polysemy are distinguished by meaning relationships under the stated convention. Matching word class is not universally required for homonymy; a sentence alone does not prove lexical history.
Bus is a hyponym of vehicle, not the reverse. Set inclusion is used to make the direction explicit. A type-of relation is separated from a part-of relation.
Metonymy is not simply defined as metaphorical replacement. Cops/police officers is treated as an informal/neutral lexical comparison, not a clear stand-for relation.
Prototype judgments concern typicality rather than automatic exclusion of less typical members. Rankings are not imposed as identical across communities.
Ambiguity questions use explicit competing senses and sufficient context. The isolated Alice quotation is not assigned an invented ambiguity unsupported by the slide.

Causative is replaced with cause/causer as a participant-role label. Theme is tested with clear moved-entity examples rather than assuming every object is physically altered. Semantic roles are distinguished from subject/object; role inventories can vary.

questions.question: What is the main concern of semantics?
questions.explanation: Semantics investigates meaning, not just whole-sentence interpretation. Smaller meaningful units and their combinations are also relevant.
questions.example: The meaning of plural -s and the meaning of a whole sentence can both be studied semantically.

options.text: The geographical distribution of accents alone
The physical production of consonants alone
Linguistic meaning at levels including morphemes, words, phrases, and sentences
The alphabetical ordering of a dictionary

questions.question: Which description correctly identifies lexical semantics?
questions.explanation: The slide incorrectly assigns larger-than-word units to lexical semantics. The lexical level concerns words and associated meaning relations.
questions.example: Comparing large and big is a lexical semantic task.

options.text: The study only of syntactic units larger than a word
The study only of punctuation between clauses
The study of tongue movements during articulation
The study of word and morpheme meanings and their relationships

questions.question: Which question most directly concerns the meaning of a phrase or sentence rather than a single lexical item?
questions.explanation: Meaning can be investigated compositionally, by examining how parts contribute to a larger expression. The alternatives focus on lexical meaning.
questions.example: The combination red bag conveys more specific content than bag alone.

options.text: What senses does the word bank have?
What does the word bag mean?
How do the meanings of words combine in “the small red bag”?
How are bag and sack related in meaning?

questions.question: Which question belongs primarily to semantics rather than acoustic phonetics?
questions.explanation: The correct question concerns linguistic interpretation. The alternatives ask about physical properties of a speech signal.
questions.example: The door is closed describes a different state from the door being open.

options.text: How long does the vowel last in the recording?
How large is the waveform amplitude?
What situation does “The door is open” describe?
Which frequency band contains the most energy?

questions.question: What distinction separates conventional sentence meaning from a speaker’s indirect request in context?
questions.explanation: The same utterance can have a conventional meaning and a contextual purpose. Semantics and pragmatics contribute different questions to its interpretation.
questions.example: It is cold here can describe temperature and be used to request closing a window.

options.text: The former is morphology; the latter is phonetic intensity.
Both exclude any role for language interpretation.
The former foregrounds semantics; the latter foregrounds pragmatics.
Both are decided only by the number of letters.

questions.question: Beside an open window, a speaker says “It is cold here” to get someone to close it. Which part of the analysis is specifically pragmatic?
questions.explanation: The request is not a direct command in the wording. It is inferred from the utterance and its circumstances.
questions.example: There is no room on this seat can indirectly ask someone to move a bag.

options.text: Inferring the intended request from the situation
Identifying cold as a word with a temperature-related meaning
Identifying the sentence as containing words
Recognizing that here is a linguistic expression

questions.question: Why can a morpheme be relevant to semantics even when it is not a complete word?
questions.explanation: A meaningful contribution can be smaller than a word. Bound endings can affect how the whole form is interpreted.
questions.example: The plural ending in books contributes a number distinction.

options.text: It can contribute lexical or grammatical meaning.
Bound morphemes have no linguistic contribution.
Meaning exists only in independent clauses.
Every morpheme must name a physical object.

questions.question: Why is semantics not adequately defined as a list of dictionary definitions?
questions.explanation: A dictionary is a useful resource, but semantic analysis asks systematic questions beyond listing entries. Combination and relations are important too.
questions.example: The meanings of dog and chased do not alone list every relation in The dog chased the cat.

options.text: Words lose all meaning when they form a sentence.
Only rare words have meanings that can be analysed.
It also investigates meaning relations and the interpretation of larger expressions.
Dictionary entries completely determine every speaker’s contextual intention.

questions.question: What does denotation concern in the introductory contrast used here?
questions.explanation: Denotation connects a linguistic expression with its referential interpretation. It differs from emotional or personal associations linked to the expression.
questions.example: Rose can denote a kind of flower while also evoking romance.

options.text: What an expression refers to or applies to
Only the politeness of a speaker’s request
Only the private memories a word evokes
Only the rhythm of a spoken phrase

questions.question: What is connotation in the lecture’s introductory discussion?
questions.explanation: Connotation concerns associations beyond basic referential content. These can be personal, cultural, or context-dependent.
questions.example: Home may evoke comfort for some users.

options.text: The exact duration of the spoken word
The number of written letters in a noun
Associations or evaluative overtones linked with an expression
The grammatical subject of every sentence

questions.question: A learner says that rose names a flower but also suggests romance. Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: The example separates what the expression applies to from an associated idea. An association need not be part of every use.
questions.example: A rose in a botanical description need not communicate romantic feelings.

options.text: Flower-related reference concerns denotation; romance is an association.
The two observations establish that rose has no conventional meaning.
Romance is the only possible denotation of rose.
The flower reference is a phonetic measurement.

questions.question: What is the extension of a category expression in a specified situation or domain?
questions.explanation: Extension identifies applicable instances in a domain. For a category term, it should not be reduced to one chosen example.
questions.example: In a supplied toy collection, the extension of red toy includes all the red toys there.

options.text: The private picture one learner happens to imagine
The set of things to which it applies
The number of syllables in its spelling
The list of emotions the sound evokes

questions.question: What is an intension in the elementary category-based account used here?
questions.explanation: Intension concerns how applicability is determined. It is distinct from extension and from a speaker’s communicative intention.
questions.example: The criteria for triangle differ from the set of triangles in a particular diagram.

options.text: The descriptive content or criteria determining what an expression applies to
Any personal association with the sound of the word
The complete set of actual examples in a chosen domain
The speaker’s communicative intention in every conversation

questions.question: Why should intension not simply be equated with a personal mental picture?
questions.explanation: An imagined example is not the same as a definition or descriptive criterion. The slide’s mental-image shorthand needs that qualification.
questions.example: Picturing a hot sandy desert does not establish that every desert must be hot and sandy.

options.text: Only words with photographs have intensions.
Every category must contain exactly the object pictured by the speaker.
A vivid image can contain incidental details that are not criteria for the category.
The most familiar example necessarily exhausts a category’s meaning.

questions.question: For a sewing needle, which information is most directly conceptual rather than a personal association?
questions.explanation: Conceptual content concerns what kind of thing the expression identifies in the specified sense. Emotional memories are associative rather than the defining use.
questions.example: A sewing needle can be described without requiring every user to fear it.

options.text: It makes one person feel anxious.
It is a slender pointed tool used in sewing.
It evokes a childhood memory.
It reminds the speaker of a frightening visit.

questions.question: A person associates needle with fear because of an earlier experience. What type of meaning is foregrounded?
questions.explanation: The feeling is linked to the person’s experience. It need not be shared by everyone who understands the word.
questions.example: Another user may associate a sewing needle with craftwork instead.

options.text: Word order
Associative meaning
Acoustic duration
Grammatical agreement

questions.question: Why is connotation alone insufficient as a complete account of conventional word meaning?
questions.explanation: Shared understanding is not identical to a set of personal reactions. The slide notes variation in associations as a limitation of an association-only account.
questions.example: Two users may understand home while responding to it differently.

options.text: All speakers necessarily have the same experiences.
Users can understand a word while having different personal associations.
A word cannot evoke an emotion if it has a referent.
Every association must be a separate phoneme.

questions.question: What challenge do fictional expressions pose for a simple account equating all meaning with an existing real-world referent?
questions.explanation: The problem concerns the completeness of a simple referential account, not a claim that every theory of denotation fails. Models can make additional provisions for fictional discourse.
questions.example: A sentence about a unicorn can be understood without locating an actual unicorn.

options.text: A meaningful expression may lack an ordinary actual-world referent and needs further explanation.
Every fictional entity must be an actual physical object.
The presence of fiction removes all conventional word meanings.
Fictional words cannot occur in grammatical sentences.

questions.question: Which comparison keeps conceptual and associative meaning distinct?
questions.explanation: These aspects can coexist in one word’s use. The distinction helps separate conventional content from additional reactions and associations.
questions.example: Hospital can identify an institution while evoking reassurance or anxiety.

options.text: Conceptual meaning is always a sound measurement; associative meaning is always word order.
Conceptual meaning belongs only to nouns; associative meaning belongs only to verbs.
The two labels refer to identical information in every context.
A basic description identifies the kind of thing; an association reflects linked feelings or ideas.

questions.question: How should the slide’s claim that linguists are uninterested in associative meaning be qualified?
questions.explanation: A focus of one introductory analysis is not a restriction on all research. The study of meaning can address several dimensions for different purposes.
questions.example: A study may investigate the evaluative overtones of words used in public debate.

options.text: Associations are excluded from every branch of linguistics.
Only associations count as linguistic meaning.
Some analyses focus on conceptual content, but associations can also be legitimate research topics.
Conceptual content makes social and emotional responses impossible.

questions.question: What is the lexicon in the lecture’s mental account?
questions.explanation: The lexicon concerns word-related linguistic knowledge. It is not identical to a paper dictionary or one acoustic recording.
questions.example: Knowing a word includes information relevant to its form and use.

options.text: A recording of every sound wave ever heard
A store of information about words and morphemes
A map of the world’s physical deserts
A list containing only printed punctuation rules

questions.question: What are semantic features or properties used for in introductory componential analysis?
questions.explanation: Feature analysis tries to make meaning relationships explicit through component properties. It is an analytical tool rather than a complete solution for every word.
questions.example: A human-related feature can distinguish some person terms from animal terms.

options.text: Measuring the sound intensity of a spoken noun
Identifying where a sentence appears on a printed page
Sorting words only by their letter count
Representing aspects of meaning that items share or contrast in

questions.question: Which set most clearly shares a human-related semantic property in its ordinary occupational senses?
questions.explanation: The occupational senses refer to people, unlike the animal, furniture, and geographical sets. Context still matters when a word has multiple uses.
questions.example: Teacher and student also have ordinary human-reference senses.

options.text: mare, hen, and tigress
table, chair, and shelf
river, desert, and valley
doctor, dean, and professor

questions.question: In their ordinary animal-reference senses, what property do mare, hen, and tigress share?
questions.explanation: A shared semantic property need not make items synonymous. The words identify different animal kinds while sharing the stated sex-related property.
questions.example: A mare and a hen are different kinds of animal despite the shared property.

options.text: They refer to female animals.
They all refer to the same species.
They are all names for human occupations.
They all mean young male animals.

questions.question: Why should doctor or professor not be assigned a male-only feature merely because of a social stereotype?
questions.explanation: Analysis should distinguish linguistic content from assumptions about typical users. A stereotype is not proof of a necessary semantic feature.
questions.example: A woman or a man can be a doctor.

options.text: A person’s occupation must determine their grammatical gender in English.
Social stereotypes determine every dictionary category.
The word’s ordinary meaning does not restrict the occupation to men.
Every occupational noun has exactly the same meaning.

questions.question: Why does sharing one semantic feature not make two words synonyms?
questions.explanation: A feature captures one dimension, not necessarily the complete meaning. Category membership and relationships can still differ.
questions.example: Mare and hen share a property but refer to different animal kinds.

options.text: Feature analysis permits only one feature per word.
Every shared property guarantees identical reference in all contexts.
Synonymy depends only on matching spelling.
Other aspects of their meanings can differ.

questions.question: What limitation of componential analysis is explicitly noted in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The method can clarify some relationships without providing a complete decomposition of all meanings. Choice and granularity of features can be difficult.
questions.example: Distinguishing color terms through a short list of discrete components may be challenging.

options.text: Feature analysis automatically predicts every contextual interpretation.
It can be difficult to specify all the features needed for a word’s meaning.
Only the spelling of a word can identify its semantic features.
Every word has exactly two uncontested meaning components.

questions.question: Why are blue and yellow useful examples when discussing limits of simple feature lists?
questions.explanation: The slide raises difficulty in identifying smaller meaning components for certain terms. This does not imply that color meaning cannot be studied.
questions.example: Researchers may need more detailed models than a short binary checklist.

options.text: Some meanings resist an obvious decomposition into a few discrete semantic parts.
Every color term must have the same extension.
A word with a color sense cannot be used in a sentence.
Color words cannot be meaningful unless users agree on spelling.

questions.question: What does semantic range refer to in the lecture’s practical discussion?
questions.explanation: A word may have different applications across contexts. The relevant interpretation must be identified rather than assuming one gloss fits every occurrence.
questions.example: Run can refer to physical movement or operating a business.

options.text: The number of letters in its longest spelling
The physical distance a sound travels
The complete list of a language’s phonemes
The range of senses or applications a word can have

questions.question: In “She runs a clinic,” which interpretation of runs fits the context?
questions.explanation: The surrounding words constrain which sense is intended. Running a clinic is not ordinarily a claim about moving it on foot.
questions.example: He runs a shop uses the same management-related sense.

options.text: Flows as a liquid
Forms a line of stitches
Moves rapidly on foot
Manages or operates

questions.question: How does point differ in “a sharp point” and “the main point of the lecture”?
questions.explanation: Context helps identify the relevant interpretation. A word’s range is not exhausted by one concrete use.
questions.example: The point of an argument differs from the point of a pencil.

options.text: The contexts select different related or conventional senses.
The second occurrence cannot have meaning because it is abstract.
The difference is only the number of letters in the word.
The word must have the same physical referent in both.

questions.question: Why is a list such as anxiety, distress, and concern not by itself an analysis of several distinct senses of worry?
questions.explanation: A list of alternatives can clarify meaning, but separate senses require evidence from use and interpretation. The slide’s example needs that caution.
questions.example: Several descriptions of unease may elaborate one sense rather than count several.

options.text: Different glosses can never help explain a word.
Every near-synonym automatically establishes a different meaning of the target word.
Related glosses can describe overlapping content without demonstrating separate senses.
A word can have a sense only if it names a physical object.

questions.question: What are selectional restrictions in this introductory discussion?
questions.explanation: Some predicates typically combine with participants of particular semantic kinds. A mismatch can make an otherwise structured sentence seem odd.
questions.example: A literal act of listening normally requires an appropriate perceiver.

options.text: A ban on every sentence containing an unfamiliar word
Semantic expectations about the kinds of participants compatible with an expression
Preferences for how a dictionary page is printed
Rules requiring every sentence to begin with a proper noun

questions.question: Why does “The table listened to music” sound odd on an ordinary literal reading?
questions.explanation: The sentence can follow a familiar syntactic pattern while conflicting with expectations about participants. Its oddness is not simply missing word order.
questions.example: A person listening to music fits the ordinary participant expectations.

options.text: A table does not ordinarily have the capacities required for listening.
The sentence has no grammatical subject.
Music cannot occur as a noun.
The verb listened lacks a past-tense form.

questions.question: Which contrast best separates syntactic well-formedness from a selectional mismatch?
questions.explanation: Grammar and semantic compatibility are different dimensions. The lecture uses odd examples to demonstrate that distinction.
questions.example: The hamburger ate the man has an ordinary arrangement but an unusual literal agent.

options.text: A well-formed sentence must describe a true event.
A selectional mismatch proves that every word is misspelled.
Any unusual event requires the absence of a verb.
A sentence can have a familiar structure while assigning an implausible participant to an action.

questions.question: A story gives a table ears and the ability to listen. How should “The table listened” be assessed in that story?
questions.explanation: Selectional judgments depend on the intended interpretation. Personification or fictional assumptions can supply capacities missing in an everyday context.
questions.example: A talking cat can study linguistics within a fictional story.

options.text: Tables must therefore be literal human agents in everyday usage.
The fictional context can support an interpretation that is odd in an ordinary literal setting.
The context removes every meaning from listened.
The sentence becomes grammatically impossible in all contexts.

questions.question: What distinction is important when a sentence is called semantically odd?
questions.explanation: A surprising literal combination may still be interpretable through a special context, metaphor, or personification. The analytical task should specify its assumptions.
questions.example: An animated film can make a sentence about a listening table understandable.

options.text: An odd sentence must be a random list of letters.
Oddness is not the same as having no possible interpretation.
Oddness proves that every speaker has an identical reaction.
A sentence about fiction is always syntactically ungrammatical.

questions.question: Why is “My cat studied linguistics” unsuitable as proof of absolute meaningless language?
questions.explanation: The slide’s point is a mismatch with ordinary participant expectations. That should not become a universal claim that no interpretation is available.
questions.example: A story about an educated animal supplies a different background.

options.text: Its spelling alone prevents any subject–verb relation.
Its ordinary-world implausibility can be overcome in a specified fictional interpretation.
The sentence contains no word with a conventional meaning.
Every cat literally studies linguistics in everyday life.

questions.question: What is synonymy in the lecture’s basic account?
questions.explanation: Synonymy concerns similarity of meaning. It need not imply that substitution works equally well in every context.
questions.example: Big and large can be close in meaning in suitable descriptions of size.

options.text: A relationship of the same or closely similar meaning between expressions
A relationship of identical form with unrelated senses
A relationship of class inclusion
A relationship of opposite meanings

questions.question: Which pair is a clear near-synonym pair in an ordinary size description?
questions.explanation: Big and large can both describe substantial size. The alternatives illustrate opposition, inclusion, and shared form with unrelated senses.
questions.example: A big house and a large house often describe similar size.

options.text: hot and cold
big and large
bus and vehicle
bank meaning money institution and bank meaning river edge

questions.question: Which pair contains verbs with closely related meanings in the intended sense?
questions.explanation: Hide and conceal can describe preventing something from being seen or discovered. The other pairs have different semantic or grammatical relationships.
questions.example: He hid the letter and he concealed the letter convey similar core content.

options.text: buy and sell
hide and conceal
car and vehicle
walk and walked

questions.question: Why should near-synonyms not be assumed interchangeable in every expression?
questions.explanation: Similarity can coexist with conventional usage differences. Context must be checked before replacing one word with another.
questions.example: Big mistake is natural, while large mistake is less usual in many ordinary contexts.

options.text: Words with similar meanings must have identical sounds.
They can differ in register, collocation, or finer shades of meaning.
Any difference in usage eliminates all meaning similarity.
A near-synonym can never occur in the same word class.

questions.question: Which example best illustrates context-sensitive synonymy?
questions.explanation: The size context supports similarity without making a universal substitution rule. Semantic comparison must specify the relevant sense.
questions.example: A big decision does not necessarily have the same normal phrasing as a large decision.

options.text: Big and large are antonyms whenever they describe buildings.
Big and large must replace each other naturally in every phrase.
Big house and large house can correspond, while fixed combinations may differ.
Two words become synonyms solely because both are short.

questions.question: Why does the lecture compare words of the same part of speech when illustrating synonymy?
questions.explanation: The examples compare like uses rather than mixing a noun sense with an unrelated verb sense. This is a practical control, not the only possible approach to semantic similarity.
questions.example: Hide and conceal are compared as verbs.

options.text: Words of different classes cannot have any semantic relationship.
Spelling alone determines every synonym relation.
Comparable grammatical uses make the intended meaning comparison clearer.
Only nouns can have closely similar meanings.

questions.question: In a context where couch and sofa name the same kind of furniture, which relation is illustrated?
questions.explanation: The two expressions have closely corresponding furniture meanings in the stated context. Dialect or stylistic preferences can still differ.
questions.example: A speaker may use either word for a familiar seating item.

options.text: Synonymy
Hyponymy between sofa and couch
Homonymy of one word
Gradable antonymy

questions.question: Which conclusion best follows from identifying two expressions as near-synonyms?
questions.explanation: Near-synonymy is a claim about meaning similarity, not total identity of every linguistic property. Context limits what the label establishes.
questions.example: Hide and conceal can be close in meaning while differing in frequency or style.

options.text: They must share the same spelling and pronunciation.
They must belong to one hierarchy as a type and its supertype.
They must have opposite truth conditions in every sentence.
Their meanings overlap substantially in the specified use, while relevant differences may remain.

questions.question: What is antonymy in the lecture’s broad introductory use?
questions.explanation: Antonymy concerns semantic contrast. Different types of oppositeness have different logical and contextual properties.
questions.example: Hot and cold are opposites along a temperature scale.

options.text: A relationship of oppositeness in meaning
A relationship of identical spelling alone
A relationship between a word and its plural form
A relationship based only on equal word length

questions.question: Which pair most clearly illustrates gradable antonymy?
questions.explanation: Hot and cold allow intermediate descriptions and degree modification. The alternatives represent other kinds of semantic relations.
questions.example: Warm and cool can occupy intermediate parts of a temperature scale.

options.text: car and bus
couch and sofa
bus and vehicle
hot and cold

questions.question: What is characteristic of gradable opposites?
questions.explanation: A scale allows more than two possible positions. Something need not count as either extreme.
questions.example: A drink can be neither hot nor cold but lukewarm.

options.text: They can describe only binary attendance decisions.
Denying one always logically guarantees the other.
They must be different names for exactly the same category.
Intermediate values and degree comparisons are possible.

questions.question: Why does “The water is not hot” not necessarily mean “The water is cold”?
questions.explanation: Negating one end of a scale does not identify the opposite end. Intermediate cases remain possible.
questions.example: Not fast can describe a moderate speed rather than a very slow one.

options.text: Not changes every adjective into its exact antonym.
Hot and cold are synonyms in negative sentences.
Water cannot be described with gradable terms.
There may be intermediate temperatures.

questions.question: In a stipulated two-state attendance system, what makes present and absent complementary labels?
questions.explanation: Complementarity depends on the specified binary classification. The example explicitly fixes the domain to avoid treating every real-world boundary as simple.
questions.example: For that coding scheme, not present is classified as absent.

options.text: Both labels are ordinary synonyms for attendance.
Every case in that system receives exactly one of the two labels.
One label names a subtype of the other.
The labels describe many intermediate degrees of attendance within that system.

questions.question: Why should complementary opposites be explained with a specified domain?
questions.explanation: A binary relation is clearest when assumptions about classification are explicit. The point should not depend on ignoring relevant contextual distinctions.
questions.example: An attendance policy must say how a late arrival is coded.

options.text: The spelling of the two words determines their logical relationship.
Complementary labels can never be useful in analysis.
Real uses may have borderline or specially defined cases that affect the contrast.
A domain automatically makes every pair gradable.

questions.question: Which relation is most directly illustrated by buy and sell when describing the same transaction from different participants’ perspectives?
questions.explanation: Buying and selling describe connected sides of one transaction. This differs from a temperature scale or a simple binary property.
questions.example: If Sara bought a book from Ali, Ali sold the book to Sara.

options.text: Converse or relational opposition
A word and its plural inflection
Unrelated homonymy
Ordinary synonymy with no perspective change

questions.question: Which statement preserves the converse relationship in “Ayesha bought the bicycle from Bilal”?
questions.explanation: The participants switch roles while the transaction remains the same. Direction of transfer is essential to the paraphrase.
questions.example: The buyer’s from relation corresponds to the seller’s to relation.

options.text: Bilal bought the bicycle from Ayesha.
Ayesha and Bilal must both have sold the bicycle to a third person.
Bilal sold the bicycle to Ayesha.
Ayesha sold the bicycle to Bilal.

questions.question: Why is teacher–pupil better treated as a role relationship than as a hot–cold type scale?
questions.explanation: The pair is relational. It does not normally support intermediate degrees between the roles in the same way as gradable adjectives.
questions.example: A person can teach one group while studying under someone else.

options.text: Both terms necessarily refer to the same role in every classroom.
The terms can identify related participants rather than opposite degrees of one property.
Every teacher must have the opposite body temperature from every pupil.
One term is always the plural of the other.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly distinguishes three kinds of opposition?
questions.explanation: The pairs differ in scale, binary classification, and participant perspective. Calling them opposites does not erase those distinctions.
questions.example: Not hot can leave an intermediate value, while buying corresponds to someone else’s selling.

options.text: Hot/cold is synonymous; present/absent is hyponymic; buy/sell is plural marking.
All three pairs are homonyms because they can occur in one sentence.
Hot/cold is gradable; binary present/absent is complementary; buy/sell is converse.
All three pairs require exactly the same scale and inference pattern.

questions.question: What contrast is central to the lecture’s examples of homonymy and polysemy?
questions.explanation: The distinction concerns the relationship among meanings, not simply the fact that several interpretations exist. Boundaries can require careful analysis.
questions.example: Bank in finance and at a river is contrasted with related senses of foot.

questions.question: Why is same spelling alone insufficient to decide whether a case is homonymy or polysemy?

questions.question: What is polysemy in the lecture’s account?

questions.question: How should the slide’s same-word-class restriction on homonymy be qualified?

questions.question: What is a hyponym?
